in.other_title: Prior-belief effects on accuracy: consultancy vs debate mixed-effects regressions
in.rationale: Michael et al. call for evaluating debate where judges have strong inaccurate priors. Rahman et al. report that under consultancy mainstream-prior judges were less accurate than skeptical ones (OR 0.70, p = 0.11), while under debate accuracy was nearly identical across prior groups (OR 1.10, p = 0.66); neither odds ratio is significant.
in.scope: proposed ADDRESSES: whether debate still works when judges hold strong possibly inaccurate priors, for COVID-19 claims

open_obligations: Check that Michael et al.'s open question concerns strong inaccurate priors, while the authors' judges include both mainstream (often correct) and skeptical believers
Confirm the debaters here are GPT-4o rather than humans, unlike Michael et al.'s main human-debater result
in.other_title: Rahman et al. extend Michael et al.'s debate-vs-consultancy test to judges with strong prior beliefs
in.rationale: The authors carry the debate-versus-consultancy comparison into the condition Michael et al. leave open (judges with strong priors or biases) and say so explicitly, which is EXTENDS. Their conclusion (p10 L31-L34) reports that debate improves accuracy and calibration over consultancy even with strong priors, but that result is outside this span.
in.scope: proposed EXTENDS: Whether debate beats consultancy when judges hold strong prior beliefs; holds for binary factuality claims with curated sources on both sides

text: Among the open problems for trustworthy AI debate, the authors state that human judges should be evaluated and trained on hard questions that exploit cognitive or social biases, where judges have strong inaccurate priors, or where the validity of evidence is hard to evaluate, to make sure debate works in such settings.
title: Does debate still work when judges hold strong inaccurate priors or cognitive biases?
